concepts.name: Two-process model
concepts.explanation: Sleep timing is explained by two interacting processes: sleep pressure that builds while awake (Process S) and the circadian clock (Process C).
concepts.caveat: It is a simplified model; mood, stress, light and behaviour also shape when and how well we sleep.
concepts.question: Why can you feel more alert at 9 pm than at 3 pm despite being awake longer?
phrases: two process model of sleep Borbely

concepts.name: Sleep pressure
concepts.explanation: The growing drive to sleep the longer you are awake, linked to the build-up of adenosine in the brain; sleep clears it.
concepts.caveat: Adenosine is one part of sleep pressure, not the full explanation.
concepts.question: Why does a long afternoon nap make it harder to fall asleep at night?

concepts.name: Circadian rhythm
concepts.explanation: A roughly 24-hour internal clock, set mainly by light, that times alertness, body temperature, hormones and sleep.
concepts.caveat: The clock is not only in the brain; organs have their own clocks that can fall out of sync, as in shift work.
concepts.question: Why is jet lag worse flying east than flying west for most people?

concepts.name: Light exposure
concepts.explanation: Light, especially bright morning daylight, is the strongest signal that sets the circadian clock; evening light shifts it later.
concepts.caveat: Screen light at night has smaller effects than often claimed compared with overall brightness and what you are doing.
concepts.question: Why might a morning walk help someone who struggles to fall asleep at night?

concepts.name: Melatonin
concepts.explanation: A hormone released in darkness that signals biological night to the body; it helps time sleep rather than forcing sleep.
concepts.caveat: Melatonin supplements are mainly useful for timing problems like jet lag, not as a strong sleeping pill.
concepts.question: Why does a melatonin tablet often help jet lag more than general insomnia?

concepts.name: Chronotype
concepts.explanation: A person's natural timing preference, from early "larks" to late "owls", partly genetic and shifting later in adolescence.
concepts.caveat: Chronotype is a spectrum, and most people are in the middle rather than strongly one type.
concepts.question: Why might school start times matter more for teenagers?

concepts.name: NREM sleep
concepts.explanation: Non-rapid eye movement sleep, divided into lighter stages and deep slow-wave sleep; it makes up most of the night.
concepts.caveat: Light NREM sleep is not "wasted" sleep; it has its own roles, including in memory.
concepts.question: Why is it harder to wake someone from deep NREM sleep than from light sleep?

concepts.name: Slow-wave sleep
concepts.explanation: The deepest stage of NREM sleep, with large slow brain waves, concentrated in the first half of the night and linked to physical recovery.
concepts.caveat: Consumer sleep trackers estimate deep sleep poorly compared with lab EEG.
concepts.question: Why does recovery sleep after a sleepless night contain extra slow-wave sleep?

concepts.name: REM sleep
concepts.explanation: Rapid eye movement sleep, with vivid dreams, an active brain and paralysed muscles; it is concentrated toward morning.
concepts.caveat: Dreams also happen outside REM, and the exact functions of REM are still debated.
concepts.question: Why might cutting sleep short by two hours cut REM sleep by much more than a quarter?

concepts.name: Sleep cycles
concepts.explanation: The night moves through repeating cycles of NREM and REM sleep, each lasting roughly 90 minutes.
concepts.caveat: Cycle length varies between people and through the night, so "wake at the end of a 90-minute cycle" is approximate.
concepts.question: Why does the balance of deep and REM sleep change across the night?

concepts.name: Memory consolidation
concepts.explanation: Sleep helps stabilise and reorganise new memories, with slow-wave sleep and spindles linked to replaying what was learned.
concepts.caveat: The effect is real but smaller and more selective than "learning while you sleep" headlines suggest.
concepts.question: Why might studying then sleeping beat studying all night before an exam?

concepts.name: Glymphatic clearance
concepts.explanation: A proposed system in which fluid flow, increased during sleep, flushes waste products from the brain.
concepts.caveat: This is an active research area; some newer studies dispute whether clearance is actually higher during sleep.
concepts.question: What evidence would show that sleep is necessary for brain waste clearance?

concepts.name: Sleep debt
concepts.explanation: The accumulated shortfall from sleeping less than you need, which impairs attention, mood and metabolism.
concepts.caveat: People adapt to feeling tired and underestimate their impairment; a weekend lie-in does not fully reverse it.
concepts.question: Why might someone sleeping 6 hours a night feel "fine" while their performance is falling?

concepts.name: Caffeine
concepts.explanation: A stimulant that blocks adenosine receptors, masking sleep pressure; its effects can last many hours.
concepts.caveat: Caffeine hides sleepiness but does not remove sleep debt, and sensitivity varies a lot between people.
concepts.question: Why might an afternoon coffee affect sleep even if you fall asleep fine?

concepts.name: Insomnia
concepts.explanation: Persistent difficulty falling or staying asleep despite the chance to sleep, causing daytime problems.
concepts.caveat: Insomnia is often kept going by worry about sleep and habits like lying awake in bed, not just the original cause.
concepts.question: Why might spending longer in bed make insomnia worse?

concepts.name: CBT-I
concepts.explanation: Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia: sleep restriction, stimulus control and changing unhelpful beliefs; it is the recommended first treatment.
concepts.caveat: It is effective long-term but often feels worse before it gets better, during sleep restriction.
concepts.question: Why does restricting time in bed help people sleep better?
